opus-5.5.text:
I see KDA as a fairly natural next step from Gated DeltaNet rather than a radical departure, and I'm happy that the Kimi team pushed it to a scale where people can actually see whether these ideas hold up.

The core of Gated DeltaNet combined two mechanisms. The delta rule gives you a targeted way to update memory: before writing a new key-value association, you first remove what's already stored along that key direction, so it behaves like online regression rather than just piling things up. The gating, borrowed from the Mamba2 line of work, lets the model decay its memory so it can forget stale information. In Gated DeltaNet the gate was a scalar per head, so the whole state decays uniformly. That was a deliberate choice for hardware efficiency, because a scalar decay keeps the chunkwise parallel algorithm simple and fast.

What KDA does is make that gate fine-grained, channel-wise along the key dimension, closer to what we had in Gated Linear Attention. So each feature dimension of the memory can have its own forgetting rate. Intuitively that's more expressive: some channels can act like long-term memory, others like short-term scratch space. Mathematically it moves you toward a diagonal-plus-low-rank transition matrix, and the general DPLR form is expensive and numerically tricky. I think the real contribution of KDA is on the systems side: constraining the structure so the chunkwise algorithm stays efficient and stable, getting much of the expressiveness of the general form without paying its full cost.

The other thing I appreciate is that they didn't claim linear attention alone is enough. They used it in a hybrid, with most layers being KDA and a few full attention layers interleaved. I think that's the honest picture right now. Linear layers are good at compressing state and handling local and medium-range structure cheaply. A small amount of global attention covers precise retrieval, which a fixed-size state fundamentally struggles with.

So for me, KDA validates the direction: the delta rule plus better forgetting, with careful kernel design. It also shows that the bottleneck is often less about inventing a new formula and more about making the formula trainable at scale on real hardware.

r001.rationale: It says Gated DeltaNet used a scalar gate per head, causing the whole state to decay uniformly, and ties that choice to hardware efficiency.

r002.rationale: It describes KDA’s gate as channel-wise along the key dimension, giving each feature dimension its own forgetting rate instead of one shared rate.

r003.rationale: It says per-channel rates are more expressive and can support long-term memory or short-term scratch space, but does not connect them to making better use of limited hidden-state capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The way I think about KDA is that it's really a direct descendant of Gated DeltaNet, but with one change that turned out to matter a lot in practice: the gating goes from scalar to per-channel.

In Gated DeltaNet, we had the delta rule, which lets the model do targeted erasure and overwriting of the state, plus a gating mechanism that decays the whole state. But that gate was a single scalar per head. Every channel in the state was forgetting at the same rate at every timestep. That's a very coarse control knob. Some dimensions might want to hold onto information for a long time while others should forget quickly, and a scalar gate can't express that.

So KDA moves to a diagonal, per-channel gate, more like what Mamba2 does with its decay, but keeping the delta rule structure. Conceptually that's a small change. The hard part was making it efficient. Once the decay is a vector rather than a scalar, the chunkwise parallel form becomes much messier, because you can no longer factor the decay out as a simple cumulative product across the chunk. The Kimi team put in a lot of engineering work to design a chunkwise algorithm, with a specialized representation, that still maps well onto tensor cores. The way I'd put it is, the fine-grained gating gives you the expressiveness, and the kernel work is what makes it actually worth doing at scale.

The other design choice I think is important is how KDA sits inside the full model. It's not a pure linear attention model. It's a hybrid, with KDA layers interleaved with global attention layers at roughly a 3-to-1 ratio. My view has been for a while that pure linear attention has a ceiling on retrieval-heavy tasks, and the best use of these layers is to handle most of the sequence processing efficiently while a small number of full attention layers do the precise lookups. So in some sense KDA validates the whole trajectory: delta rule for memory management, gating for forgetting, make the gating finer-grained, hybridize with softmax attention, and then invest heavily in the kernels so it's actually faster at long context.

What I find satisfying is that it's a case where the research line held up when someone took it to a much larger scale than I could run myself. The ideas were there in Gated DeltaNet; KDA shows what they look like with a bigger training budget and more careful systems work.

r001.rationale: The response says Gated DeltaNet used one scalar gate per head and explains that this makes decay easier to factor across a chunk. It does not clearly state that the shared rate was chosen for computational efficiency.

r002.rationale: It explicitly contrasts Gated DeltaNet’s single scalar gate per head with KDA’s diagonal, per-channel gate.

r003.rationale: It says per-channel gating lets dimensions retain or forget information at different rates, but does not connect this to making better use of the RNN’s limited hidden-state capacity.

astra-6.text:
I’d think of KDA as a refinement of the same idea behind Gated DeltaNet: combining a delta-rule memory update with a mechanism for forgetting.

The delta rule makes the update depend on what the memory already contains. You read out what’s stored for the current key, compare that with the value you want to store, and write back the correction. Gating adds another capability: deciding how much of the existing memory to retain.

In Gated DeltaNet, that forgetting is controlled by a scalar gate per head at each token. So within a head, the memory decays at the same rate. KDA makes that control finer-grained, using a channel-wise gate. Different parts of the memory can have different retention rates, rather than sharing one decay factor.

That’s the central relationship: KDA keeps the delta-rule update, but makes forgetting more expressive. And the practical design challenge is to support that extra flexibility while preserving efficient, hardware-friendly training and recurrent inference.

r001.rationale: It says Gated DeltaNet uses one scalar gate per head, so the memory decays at one rate within the head, but it does not say this was chosen for computational efficiency.

r002.rationale: It contrasts Gated DeltaNet’s shared per-head decay with KDA’s channel-wise gates, which allow different parts of memory to have different retention rates.

r003.rationale: It does not connect KDA’s finer-grained decay rates to making better use of the RNN’s limited hidden-state capacity.

sol-6.1.text:
I see KDA as a continuation of the idea behind Gated DeltaNet. The core question is the same: how do we let a recurrent memory forget outdated information while still updating it precisely?

In Gated DeltaNet, the gate controls how much of the old state we retain, while the delta rule makes the update corrective: we write the difference between what the memory currently predicts and what we want it to store. Those are two complementary mechanisms—forgetting and correction.

KDA makes the forgetting mechanism more expressive by moving from a scalar gate to a channel-wise gate. Instead of asking the whole memory to decay at the same rate, different channels can retain information over different timescales. That gives the model finer control over what it keeps and what it replaces.

So I would emphasize the continuity: KDA preserves the delta-rule foundation and makes the control over memory more fine-grained. The engineering challenge is to turn that additional expressiveness into an efficient implementation, so the benefit survives at the level of actual training and inference.

r001.rationale: It says Gated DeltaNet uses a scalar gate so the whole memory decays at the same rate, but does not specify that this rate is shared across dimensions within each attention head for computational efficiency.

r002.rationale: It describes KDA’s shift to channel-wise gates and different timescales, but does not clearly state that it replaces a rate shared within each attention head with a separate rate for every dimension.

r003.rationale: It does not connect per-dimension decay rates to making better use of the RNN’s limited hidden-state capacity.
